item.title: Framing the News: Anti-Piracy Press Release Turned a 2016 Raid Into a 2026 Story (2016)
item.description:
Home > Opinion Articles >

In August, City of London Police and anti-piracy group FACT announced a six and a half year prison sentence for a 68-year-old pirate IPTV operator. Without dates or a service name in the release, some outlets reported it as a recent bust. Records obtained by TorrentFreak show the operation was raided in 2016, the operator pleaded guilty, and the service was called Ex Pat TV.

On August 27, City of London Police published a press release headlined: “Man in his 60s jailed for 6.5 years after making over £980,000 through illegal streaming.”

In the days that followed, this exact framing was repeated throughout many online news articles.

The release came with statements from the Federation Against Copyright Theft (FACT), the Premier League, Sky and BBC Studios. Additionally, FACT published the same release on its own website the next day.

Headlines

City of London Police said that a 68-year-old from Chorley was “found guilty of conspiracy to defraud” at Preston Crown Court. His business ran on 80 servers, sold subscriptions to customers worldwide, particularly British expats, and generated £980,812 “over a three-year period.”

As is often the case with UK enforcement efforts, details are scarce. The official press releases didn’t mention the pirate service at stake, nor did they say anything about when these offenses took place, or what the reasoning of the court was.

Some news reports filled in these blanks themselves. The Mirror, for example, used the following headline: “Massive streaming crackdown blocks more UK homes from watching Sky for free.”

The Mirror reported that a “major closure has taken place after a man behind a popular illegal streaming service was recently arrested.” The server seizure left customers “with nothing more than blank screens,” it added, suggesting that this was a recent action.

The Mirror, September 1

IBC reported that all 80 servers “have now been seized,” and a French site wrote that British justice had “just dismantled” the operation. Meanwhile, BleepingComputer suggested the seized servers “may lead to the identification of users” who could face fines.

After some digging, we can now confirm that this case isn’t recent at all. In fact, the raid on Ibrahim’s operation dates back to 2016, more than a decade ago.

Pleaded Guilty

The release got the three-year period right, but the rest of the picture looks different.

After several emails and a check of our press credentials, Preston Crown Court confirmed that Ibrahim pleaded guilty to two counts. For the indictment, the court referred us to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which also named the service and answered follow-up questions, partly on background.

According to the CPS, Ibrahim pleaded guilty five days into his trial.

A guilty plea sounds different than being “found guilty”. When we asked the City of London Police about the wording in its press release, it said: “The jury did find him guilty but he plead guilty before. The terminology is fine to use for either.”

When a defendant changes his plea after the jury has been sworn in, the jury is typically asked to return a formal guilty verdict. The conviction rests on the plea.

Which Three Years?

The indictment also fills in the dates, revealing that this case is far from new. All three counts run from June 1, 2013 to August 10, 2016.

That end date is the day of a raid. On August 10, 2016, PIPCU searched a business and three homes in Chorley and arrested three men, aged 36, 40 and 58, on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud and money laundering. Ibrahim was 58 at the time. The 2026 release does not mention this raid.

From the indictment

TorrentFreak reported on the raid the next day. At the time, sources already pointed to a Chorley company selling IPTV packages to expats.

The CPS now confirms that the previously unnamed service was “initially known as ‘Ex Pat TV’ and latterly ‘My TV Abroad’.” This rebrand happened before the raid.

With those names, TorrentFreak was able to locate the service’s old website. An archived copy of mytvabroad.com from July 15, 2016, less than four weeks before the raid, carries a banner announcing the switch: “BIG RE-BRAND! Ex-Pat TV is now My TV Abroad.”

My TV Abroad, July 2016

The site promised “live UK channels, anywhere in the world” from £19 per month, with no VPN required. Its footer credits a web designer in Chorley.

That means FACT’s identification of the service, which it highlighted in the release, took place more than a decade ago. That wasn’t mentioned either. There’s more new information too.

From Three Defendants to One

The press release mentions just one defendant, but the indictment names three. In addition to Milan Ibrahim, it lists two other men, who were also charged with conspiracy to defraud copyright holders, through live TV streams, movie streams and satellite decoders supplied to commercial premises.

Milan Ibrahim pleaded guilty to the first two counts but the other two men were not convicted. The Crown did not proceed against either of them. TorrentFreak understands that Milan Ibrahim was seen as the main instigator, and that the case against the other two was resolved as part of his plea. The exact arrangement hasn’t been confirmed.

None of the new information changes the outcome. Ibrahim is serving six and a half years and, according to the police, faces Proceeds of Crime Act proceedings to recover the £980,812. That was all clear from the press release.

For proper news reporting, however, context is key. That the pirate IPTV service, Ex Pat TV or My TV Abroad, was raided a decade ago, and that the sentence followed a guilty plea, are not trivial details. The same is true for the co-defendants, who were part of the same indictment.

Why the police and FACT left these details out is unknown.

—

A copy of the revised indictment in R v Ibrahim and others (Preston Crown Court, T20237377) is available here (pdf). The names of the two co-defendants, who were not convicted, have been redacted.

item.title: Meta Pitches AI Sports Piracy Detector in Notorious Markets Rebuttal
item.description:
Home > Law and Politics >

Meta informed the U.S. Trade Representative that it built an AI tool to predict whether a live stream is a pirated sports broadcast. The tool is featured in Meta’s rebuttal to this year’s “notorious markets” submissions, which also lists restrictions on Facebook Live. Cloud storage platform Mega, meanwhile, rejects piracy accusations in its rebuttal but acknowledges that its repeat infringer system didn't work properly for months.

Earlier this month, rightsholders sent their annual overviews of “notorious” piracy markets to the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR).

The MPA, RIAA and other groups listed dozens of pirate sites, but online platforms and infrastructure providers were mentioned too. Several of them have now responded with rebuttals of their own.

This includes Meta, whose rebuttal mostly addresses counterfeiting concerns. However, unlike last year, the company also dedicates a section to piracy, much of it focused on unauthorized live streams.

AI-Predicted Pirate Streams

Meta describes a three-pronged response to piracy. It aims to stop infringing content from being posted, remove what gets through, and make the rest harder to find. According to the company, its recent efforts against live streaming piracy show that this approach works.

The most prominent example is a new AI tool that spots pirated sports broadcasts while they are being streamed.

“[I]n 2026, we built and launched an advanced AI enforcement tool that analyzes video content along with additional signals, to predict whether the content is an unauthorized stream of a professional sports broadcast,” Meta writes.

“Based on the prediction results, we can proactively remove this content in real time, before it gains a significant audience, and without a rights holder ever having to intervene.”

AI enforcement

Meta doesn’t share any figures on the AI tool, such as how many streams it removed or which sports events it was used for.

IPTV and Firestick Warnings

The AI tool works alongside changes to Facebook Live. New accounts are not allowed to use Live at all, and most users can only host a limited number of streams at the same time. Accounts that had a live stream blocked are limited in the features they can use.

Meta also limits the distribution of likely infringing live content and has introduced delays, so its anti-piracy measures can take effect before a stream is visible to the public.

Beyond live streams, Meta says that the vast majority of its removals of content promoting illegal streaming devices and services now happen proactively. It also shows warning pop-ups when users search for terms such as “firestick loaded” or “iptv free.” We spotted similar warnings for IPTV searches in 2023.

Pop-ups

Meta isn’t the only company that used its rebuttal to address piracy claims.

Mega’s Suspension System Went Down

Earlier this month, the RIAA listed Mega as a cyberlocker, claiming that it fails to prevent re-uploads of infringing material or deter repeat infringement. Mega responded with a rebuttal on October 20.

The company argues that it is a cloud storage platform, not a cyberlocker. It also points to its repeat infringer policy, under which accounts that receive three strikes within six months are suspended.

However, the filing also acknowledges that this system didn’t always work.

“Because of a technical error, the suspension system did not operate fully in Q4 2024 or at all in Q1 2025,” Mega writes.

Technical error

This isn’t news to those who read Mega’s transparency report, where the outage is disclosed in two footnotes. According to the report, the issue was resolved in early April 2025.

Mega says that rightsholders who report a file can choose to have every copy removed from all accounts that store it, and it encourages the RIAA and its member labels to use this.

Mega is new on this year’s RIAA list. Cloudflare, on the other hand, has been responding to similar claims for a decade.

Groundhog Day, Again

Rightsholder groups have mentioned Cloudflare in their submissions for years, and the company has filed rebuttals since 2016. Last year, we described this back and forth as an anti-piracy Groundhog Day.

This year, Cloudflare makes its main point with the exact same sentence it used last year.

“We firmly believe that the continued use of the Notorious Markets process to pressure Cloudflare and other Internet infrastructure companies into taking actions neither expected nor required by U.S. law is both misguided and a misuse of this vital trade tool,” Cloudflare writes.

Cloudflare Flags Misuse

Other submissions and rebuttals also include repetitive or identical sections, suggesting that many piracy disputes and complaints remain unresolved.

The USTR will now review the original submissions and these and other rebuttals, to decide what warrants a mention. Its final list of notorious markets is expected to come out early next year.

—

Meta’s rebuttal is available here (pdf), Mega’s rebuttal can be found here (pdf), and Cloudflare’s response is here (pdf).

item.title: Judge Allows Google, Yahoo and Microsoft Subpoenas to Identify Gay-Torrents Users
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

FlavaWorks can subpoena Google, Yahoo, Microsoft and three other companies to identify staff and members of the defunct BitTorrent site Gay-Torrents.org, an Illinois federal court ruled. Instead of starting from IP addresses, the subpoenas target the email accounts that are linked to their tracker profiles. How FlavaWorks obtained those email addresses remains unclear.

Earlier this year, adult entertainment company FlavaWorks sued the operators and hundreds of users of private torrent tracker Gay-Torrents.org.

The lawsuit had an immediate effect, as the tracker went offline shortly after. In an amended complaint, FlavaWorks later narrowed its list of targeted users from 325 to 39.

Several of the site’s administrators and most of the targeted members are still listed as anonymous John Does. To change that, FlavaWorks asked the court for permission to subpoena their email providers. In an October 14 order, U.S. District Judge John Robert Blakey granted this request in part.

Subpoenas Target Google, Yahoo, Microsoft

The order allows FlavaWorks to subpoena Google, Yahoo, Microsoft, AT&T, Cloudflare and Newfold Digital. Each subpoena is limited to the email addresses or domains of defendants linked to that provider.

The targeted services are asked to hand over the subscriber’s name, mailing address and phone number, as well as any secondary, recovery or two-factor authentication email addresses. FlavaWorks can also request the most recent IP address that was used to access each account, covering the period from January 2025 onward.

The order

The judge didn’t give FlavaWorks carte blanche. The company also asked for the billing names and addresses on file with the email providers, and for a subpoena to payment processor Stripe to identify the people behind a Bulgarian company linked to the site. The order includes neither.

An IP Address Is Not a Person

Subpoenas targeting email providers are not common in torrent-related lawsuits. Rightsholders typically collect IP addresses from torrent swarms and ask Internet providers to identify the account holders. FlavaWorks says it has IP address data for the defendants too, but it chose to go after their email accounts instead, bypassing the more common ISP route.

As justification, FlavaWorks mentions an argument that’s usually reserved for defendants, stating that an IP address is not a person.

“But an IP address identifies an Internet subscription, not a person: it resolves to whoever pays the bill for a household, an office, a university network, or a shared carrier-grade address pool, and it can be masked by a VPN,” FlavaWorks writes.

Not a person

An email address, the company argues, is personal to the account holder, which should help to identify the defendants.

According to the exhibit filed with the motion, 22 defendants are linked to Gmail addresses, nine to Yahoo, three to Hotmail and one to an AT&T address. Two others use private domains, registered through Cloudflare and Bluehost, a Newfold Digital company.

Email providers

This list of targets isn’t limited to regular members. Several of the site’s administrators are on it as well, identified by Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail addresses. One other administrator, who used a ProtonMail address, was left out, as the Swiss company is beyond the reach of a U.S. subpoena.

Tracker Users Can Still Object

The new order doesn’t mean that the data will be handed over right away. It explicitly allows the defendants and the providers to move to quash the subpoenas.

Google, for example, has pushed back before. In February, we reported that the company raised First Amendment concerns over a similar FlavaWorks subpoena targeting users of another private tracker.

However, in a July filing, FlavaWorks said that Google produced subscriber data in that case in April. Whether that covered all the targeted Gmail accounts is not mentioned. FlavaWorks adds that the tech giant handed over the same type of information in an earlier case, without objection.

Insider Knowledge?

For FlavaWorks, the subpoenas are meant to confirm its existing suspicions. The member defendants in this case were selected because the email address on their tracker account matched an account on one of FlavaWorks’ own sites.

In a September status report, the company said that its own records already point to a probable identity for many of them. It doesn’t want to name anyone publicly, however, before the email providers confirm who is behind each account.

How FlavaWorks obtained the email addresses in the first place is still a mystery. On an invite-only tracker, this information is typically only visible to staff. The court filings don’t offer a direct answer but cite the company’s own records and “investigation” without going into detail.

The September status report, which we haven’t seen reported anywhere, shows that FlavaWorks has help, presumably from an insider.

“Plaintiff has also obtained the cooperation of an individual with direct knowledge of the Site’s operation,” it reads.

Direct knowledge

The report doesn’t say when this cooperation started, or whether this person is the source of the email addresses. That said, FlavaWorks expects that this cooperation can help identify the operators, as well as other users who shared its works or funded the site.

Some defendants are already settling. FlavaWorks notes that several members resolved the claims before they were named. Additionally, in its separate RICO lawsuit against 75 members, one John Doe agreed to pay an undisclosed settlement amount in installments.

For now, the account holders and the subpoenaed companies can still ask the court to quash the subpoenas, but the docket shows no movement on that front yet.

—

A copy of Judge Blakey’s order is available here (pdf). FlavaWorks’ renewed motion for expedited discovery, with the defendant-to-provider table, can be found here (pdf), and the September status report is available here (pdf). FlavaWorks’ July discovery motion, which mentions Google’s earlier productions, can be found here (pdf).

item.title: Streamed, the Live Sports Engine Behind Many Pirate Sites, Shuts Down
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

Live sports piracy service Streamed, which offered streams to many pirate sites, has surprisingly shut down. Its operators posted a brief farewell message without further detail, pointing visitors to five alternative sites. Earlier this month, the MPA marked the service as a growing threat in its submission to the U.S. Trade Representative.

Pirate sports streaming sites come and go, but there are a few services that have played a more central and stable role.

These “Piracy-as-a-Service” providers offer ready-made video players that other sites can embed. This allows new pirate sites to launch live sports coverage without hosting any streams themselves.

Streamed was one of these providers. The platform focused on live sports and was used as the backbone by many other sites. However, its homepage now suggests that this has come to an abrupt end.

“We are no longer operating Streamed. Thank you for the support over the years,” the message reads.

Streamed closure

The operators don’t explain why they decided to pull the plug.

Pointing to Rivals

The notice isn’t limited to streamed.pk. The strmd.link domain redirects to the closure page and streamed.st shows the same message.

404

item.title: Accused Impostor in Private Tracker Lawsuit Faces Contempt for Withholding Passport
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits >

The alleged impostor behind a lawsuit against several private torrent trackers now faces a request to hold him in civil contempt. According to the defense, he missed a deadline to hand over his passport, driver’s license, and Copyright Office paperwork. Meanwhile, the defense’s proposed discovery has blanks the missing documents were meant to fill, in addition to a subpoena for his PACER IP addresses, and requests for any AI prompts.

Last year, we reported that a filmmaker named Matthew Schneider obtained a DMCA subpoena through a California federal court, seeking information from Cloudflare on several prominent private trackers.

These trackers, including PassThePopcorn, BroadcasTheNet, Karagarga, HDBits, and Beyond-HD, allegedly shared several of his works without permission.

A few months later, the same operators were sued in an Illinois federal court. That case took a turn when defense attorneys presented evidence that the plaintiff may be an impostor, and last month the person litigating as Matthew Schneider dropped the lawsuit.

That isn’t the end of it though, as Judge Andrea R. Wood kept jurisdiction over the pending sanctions request. Before any sanctions can follow, the defense wants the court to verify the identity of the plaintiff.

At a September hearing, the man said that Matthew Schneider is his legal name and that he lives in London. In response, the court requested official paperwork to back that up.

Passport, License, Copyright Application

Judge Wood had ordered the October 2 status hearing to take place by videoconference, but the plaintiff joined by phone, noting that he had technical difficulties.

At the hearing, the judge directed him to email the courtroom deputy copies of his driver’s license, his passport, and documentation of his application to the U.S. Copyright Office by October 9.

The documents would be filed under seal and shared with the parties under a protective order. However, the deadline seemingly passed without a response.

On October 14, the plaintiff asked the court if he could share a single “independently certified and apostilled” UK government photo ID instead, to be examined by the judge alone with no access for the defense.

These privacy restrictions are warranted, he argues, citing UK data protection law. Once his government ID is exposed, he adds, that can’t be undone.

“Once opposing counsel receives Plaintiff’s sensitive government-issued identification and residential information, the resulting loss of confidentiality cannot meaningfully be reversed,” the motion reads.

‘In lieu of producing both a passport and driving licence’

If the court refuses to restrict the disclosure, he asks for a temporary stay so he can seek appellate review. The motion does not mention the Copyright Office records, however, which as far as the defense knows haven’t been shared either.

‘This Is Plaintiff’s Design’

Two days later, Erin Russell, who represents Doe 1, asked Judge Wood to order the plaintiff to explain why he shouldn’t be held in civil contempt. According to the motion, he had agreed on the record to hand over the documents.

Russell isn’t asking for punishment, at least not yet. She wants a sworn statement on what was sent and when, followed by an in-person hearing.

The identity question is more than a formality. As Russell told the court in September, any sanctions award would be uncollectible unless the court first establishes who the plaintiff actually is.

In a filing last week, Doe 1 went a step further. “Plaintiff’s refusal to produce his passport and driving license hinders the discovery plan agreed to by the parties on October 2, 2026. Defendants do not know Plaintiff’s true identity,” it reads.

The plaintiff already made it clear that he will appeal if his motion is denied, which would drag this case further along. According to Doe 1’s filing, this is no accident.

“This interference with the discovery schedule is not incidental. This is Plaintiff’s design.”

Plaintiff’s design

Blanks to Fill

In last week’s filing, Doe 1 shared its proposed discovery requests and subpoenas. Doe #10, identified in its own filing as Usenet indexer omgwtfnzbs.org, submitted a similar filing. Both are incomplete, as the defense doesn’t have the identity documents.

Doe #10 had planned to tailor its requests to the passport, license, and copyright paperwork. Without them, it switched to placeholders such as “Admit that Your legal name is [insert legal name on passport].”

Placeholders

The proposed subpoenas target Google for the plaintiff’s Gmail account, the carrier of his phone number, and the mailbox provider or landlord for his Sanborn, New York address. From the latter, Doe 1 seeks billing records, payment methods, and the addresses to which his mail is “allegedly forwarded.”

Doe 1 also wants the PACER Service Center to hand over the IP addresses the plaintiff used to access the court’s website.

The defendants are also measuring their own exposure. Both Does ask for “all documents, data, and other materials” he received from the companies he subpoenaed since August 2025.

According to the filings, that includes materials Cloudflare produced in response to the California DMCA subpoena. The exhibit they cite, which the plaintiff filed in February, is currently sealed.

Previously, Doe 1’s attorney suggested that the person behind the lawsuit had been banned from the trackers and “bears ill will” over it, hinting at a retaliatory motive.

Was ‘Do Us Part’ Made With AI?

The last set of questions deals with “Do Us Part,” one of three films the plaintiff says he made in the UK. After being ordered by the court, he submitted his version of the film in September. According to his motion, the evidence “directly refuted” the claim that his film is the Canadian production.

His film was allegedly created more than 14 years ago, but the defense appears to doubt this. They ask the plaintiff to admit that the submission “was generated, in whole or in part, using GenAI.”

GenAI

They also want the original file, all raw footage, and “all prompts, outputs, project files, account records, and activity logs” for any use of AI.

All parties can still file objections to the discovery requests and they are scheduled to meet again at a video hearing on November 17. This time, the court has directed the plaintiff to test his video capabilities before it starts.

—

The plaintiff’s motion to modify the ID order is available here (pdf). Doe 1’s contempt motion is here (pdf). The proposed discovery requests from Doe 1 and Doe #10 can be found here (pdf) and here (pdf).

item.title: Chile Blocks 1,954 Pirate TV URLs to Protect Citizens’ ‘Privacy and Personal Data’ (1954)
item.description:
Home > Anti-Piracy > Site Blocking >

Chile's telecoms regulator Subtel reports that local ISPs blocked 1,954 pirate streaming URLs between June and October. The blocks are part of a court order obtained by Warner Bros., but Subtel presents them as a data protection measure. Meanwhile, the piracy problem persists as several of the targeted brands remain just a search away.

Early this year, a Santiago court sided with Warner Bros. in its fight against MagisTV, FlujoTV, and XuperTV, three popular Latin American pirate streaming brands.

The 19th Civil Court of Santiago ordered all variants of these services to be blocked and instructed telecoms regulator Subtel to notify the country’s Internet providers. Subtel sent these blocking orders in January, and Warner later followed up with a criminal complaint against a local IPTV operator.

This week, new info released by Subtel shows that these initial blocking measures were just the beginning, as the blocking campaign continues to expand.

According to the regulator, the ISPs GTD, DirecTV, Entel, WOM, Mundo, ClaroVTR, Netline, and Movistar have now blocked a total of 1,954 URLs linked to illegal IPTV services. These blocklist updates come in batches, which come in regularly.

URLs blocked per month

Month URLs Share
June 221
July 180
August 469
September 319
October 765
Total 1,954

The blocked domains are not limited to MagisTV, FlujoTV, and XuperTV. Subtel also lists Cuevana, Oleada TV, Stella TV, TeleLatino, PelisPlus, Cinecalidad, and Fútbol Libre, as well as their variants and mirror sites.

Subtel’s announcement came shortly after Chilean police arrested 16 people linked to the pirate IPTV services UltraIPTV and MegaIPTV, in a separate criminal investigation.

A Matter of Data Protection

Subtel’s announcement doesn’t lead with copyright. Its headline puts digital security and data protection first, and the regulator says the procedure aims to protect citizens’ privacy and personal data.

Digital safety first (translated)

Subtel warns that these unauthorized streaming platforms can collect sensitive data from users, leaving them exposed to cybercrime, data theft, and financial fraud.

“By installing these informal apps, users expose their bank passwords, personal data, and devices to hacks and scams, without any kind of support or protection,” says Undersecretary of Telecommunications Romina Garrido (translated).

“When using a pirate app or site, users hand over the key to their personal data to unknown organizations,” Garrido adds.

The data protection argument isn’t new. Warner’s own legal action argued that the pirate platforms put users’ personal data at risk, local media reported in February.

Garrido also points users to legal alternatives. “With these blocks, we break the chain of cybercrime and promote a legal offering that actually guarantees data protection and support, such as the one offered by Chile’s formal telecommunications industry,” she says.

MagisTV and Beyond

While the court order serves as the legal basis for the blocks, the original ruling only named MagisTV, FlujoTV, and XuperTV, according to reports at the time. Since then, the piracy blocklist has expanded considerably.

According to La Tercera, other pirate TV sites were added based on an interpretation of the ruling. Subtel, the Public Prosecutor’s Office, Warner, and the Alliance Against Digital Piracy then agreed on a protocol to decide which sites should be blocked.

Subtel’s monthly figures start in June, months after the regulator notified ISPs in January. The regulator didn’t explain the gap, but it’s possible that the protocol took some time to put in place.

In practice, the anti-piracy Alliance puts together the lists of URLs, IP addresses, and domains. Subtel then forwards these to the ISPs, which implement the blocks nationwide.

The order itself is quite broad. According to Emol, it covers all variants of the three brands, including any domain, subdomain, IP address, link, redirect, or mirror site that reproduces audiovisual content, wholly or partially, without authorization.

Whac-El-Topo

Despite the growing list, the blocking efforts haven’t stopped piracy. BioBioChile found that several of the targeted sites are still online.

Our own search shows that alternatives and copycats remain easy to find as well, including sites that use the popular Cuevana, Fútbol Libre, and MagisTV brands.

MagisTV search

As shown earlier, October is the busiest month so far, with 765 blocked URLs and several days still to go. That number will likely rise further as the game of whac-a-mole continues.

item.title: Vietnam Indicts HiAnime Operators Over $12.85 Million in Pirate Ad Revenue (Updated)
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits >

Vietnam's top prosecutor has indicted seven alleged HiAnime operators, sending them to trial for copyright infringement and money laundering. According to the indictment, the group behind the anime piracy ring collected $12.85 million in USDT through ad network PropellerAds. The crypto was allegedly laundered and spent on property and luxury cars, including a Porsche, a Mercedes G63 and a Land Rover.

With more than 150 million monthly visits, HiAnime was one of the most popular piracy portals to ever exist.

The anime streaming giant, previously known as Zoro.to and Aniwatch, shut down in March without offering an explanation.

Four months later, Vietnamese police arrested four of its alleged operators, and charged seven people in total.

The authorities didn’t name the site at the time, but we identified it through footage aired by state broadcaster VTV. Vietnam’s Supreme People’s Procuracy now names HiAnime directly, in an indictment that also reveals where the money came from.

Seven Defendants Head to Trial

Today, the procuracy indicted Nguyễn Đình Minh Khoa and six co-defendants, who will be tried by the Hanoi People’s Court. Khoa, Nguyễn Trung Anh, Nguyễn Hoàng Thanh and Nguyễn Đình Xuân are charged with copyright infringement and money laundering. The other three only face copyright infringement charges.

The defendants

According to state news agency TTXVN, the case originated with a complaint filed with the Ministry of Public Security by Rouse, the law firm that represents the Motion Picture Association (MPA) in Vietnam.

This complaint was filed on May 7, which was also the first day of a nationwide crackdown on pirate sites, triggered by an urgent order from Vietnam’s Prime Minister.

The HiAnime investigation eventually traced the operation back to early 2019, when Khoa allegedly came up with the idea to build pirate streaming sites that were easier to use than existing ones.

Khoa reportedly bought more than 100 domain names and worked on search engine optimization. Trung Anh managed the servers, Xuân programmed the sites, and Thanh designed them and handled the payouts. To expand the operation, co-defendant Nguyễn Phước Toàn was allegedly put in charge of the Zoro, Aniwatch and HiAnime pages on Reddit.

HiAnime wasn’t the only brand. The indictment also mentions Sflix/Myflixerz and 9animetv. Between mid-2019 and March 2026, the group allegedly offered 26,000 TV series and 7,500 anime titles through its network of sites.

12.85 Million USDT Through PropellerAds

The prosecution says that Khoa was in charge of the advertising. He allegedly dealt with advertising platform PropellerAds via Skype and Telegram, and placed its ads on the various pirate sites.

“Through the Propeller Ads platform, the defendants received a total of 12.85 million USDT, equivalent to 12.85 million USD,” Báo Bảo vệ pháp luật’s report reads (translated).

According to TTXVN, PropellerAds paid out 12.85 million USDT which was sent to the group’s crypto wallets.

The indictment notes that Khoa personally received 2.5 million USDT from 2020 onward, while Thanh collected 10.35 million USDT through wallets on the Binance exchange starting in September 2023. After costs, the four main defendants split the profits equally, which earned each of them at least 50 billion Vietnamese dong, roughly $2 million.

PropellerAds has been criticized by Hollywood before. The MPA recommended the advertising company for the USTR’s annual notorious markets list, arguing that many pirate sites use it to generate revenue. PropellerAds rejected these claims and, in 2023, accused the MPA of harassment and defamation.

Whether PropellerAds was aware of HiAnime’s activities is unknown.

Update: After publication, PropellerAds’ attorney Val Gurvits sent us a statement on behalf of the company. PropellerAds says it is an intermediary between advertisers and publishers that “does not host, produce, control or endorse the content of publishers’ websites.”

“Propeller does not tolerate copyright-infringing content and it carefully processes any copyright abuse notices filed through its abuse form available on their website,” the statement adds.

The company declined to comment on the HiAnime case itself. “Regarding the case in Vietnam, as a matter of policy, Propeller does not comment on individual publisher accounts, payment information or allegations made in ongoing legal proceedings, which have yet to be tested in court,” Gurvits writes.

The attorney adds that PropellerAds is not a party in the Vietnamese proceedings and “had no involvement in the ownership, operation or management of HiAnime.”

Cloudflare Storage, DMCA Subpoenas

The indictment also mentions other intermediaries. Trung Anh allegedly rented servers from hosting company Evoluso between 2019 and 2022. From 2023 until March 2026, the group’s storage system relied on services from Cloudflare.

The MPA previously tried to identify the people behind HiAnime through Cloudflare. In October 2024, it requested a DMCA subpoena requiring the company to share information on hianime.to and several related domains. A year later, it requested another one, listing a new batch of HiAnime branded domains.

Whether these subpoenas produced any information that helped the Vietnamese investigation is unknown.

From Porsche to G63

Over the years, the sites repeatedly received DMCA copyright warnings from Google, prosecutors say. However, the defendants kept changing the site addresses, so they could continue streaming and collecting ad revenue. This matches with the rebranding efforts.

Early this year, the defendants allegedly began to cover their tracks. In February, fearing detection, Trung Anh had his sister register his Porsche in her name. Xuân did the same with a Mercedes, which he registered to his father and later his sister, while also changing its license plate.

By March 2026, as the authorities stepped up their action against copyright infringement, the defendants decided to stop operating and deleted the websites they had used,” Báo Bảo vệ pháp luật reports (translated).

HiAnime’s goodbye in March

Vietnam's top prosecutor has indicted seven alleged HiAnime operators, sending them to trial for copyright infringement and money laundering. The crypto was allegedly laundered and spent on property and luxury cars, including a Porsche, a Mercedes G63 and a Land Rover.

With more than 150 million monthly visits, HiAnime was one of the most popular piracy portals to ever exist.

The anime streaming giant, previously known as Zoro.to and Aniwatch, shut down in March without offering an explanation.

Four months later, Vietnamese police arrested four of its alleged operators, and charged seven people in total.

The authorities didn’t name the site at the time, but we identified it through footage aired by state broadcaster VTV. Vietnam’s Supreme People’s Procuracy now names HiAnime directly, in an indictment that also reveals where the money came from.

Seven Defendants Head to Trial

Today, the procuracy indicted Nguyễn Đình Minh Khoa and six co-defendants, who will be tried by the Hanoi People’s Court. Khoa, Nguyễn Trung Anh, Nguyễn Hoàng Thanh and Nguyễn Đình Xuân are charged with copyright infringement and money laundering. The other three only face copyright infringement charges.

The defendants

According to state news agency TTXVN, the case originated with a complaint filed with the Ministry of Public Security by Rouse, the law firm that represents the Motion Picture Association (MPA) in Vietnam.

This complaint was filed on May 7, which was also the first day of a nationwide crackdown on pirate sites, triggered by an urgent order from Vietnam’s Prime Minister.

The HiAnime investigation eventually traced the operation back to early 2019, when Khoa allegedly came up with the idea to build pirate streaming sites that were easier to use than existing ones.

item.title: Ex-Meta Researcher Torrented Pirated Books Dataset, Deleted It ‘Due to All This Litigation’
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits >

A former Meta researcher has testified that he downloaded an AI training dataset via BitTorrent, including the pirated Books3 collection. According to various rightsholders, this happened while he worked at the company, and he later deleted his copy "[d]ue to all this litigation." Meta, which admitted training AI models on Books3 but said it didn’t believe it torrented the dataset, disputes the researcher’s account.

In a series of lawsuits in California federal court, Meta is being sued over the use of pirated books to train its Llama AI models.

The lawsuits are separate, but Judge Vince Chhabria handles them together. The plaintiffs include authors such as Sarah Silverman and Ta-Nehisi Coates, and publishers such as Entrepreneur Media and Chicken Soup for the Soul.

In August, Meta told Entrepreneur that it did not believe it had obtained the pirated Books3 dataset through BitTorrent. Books3 is a collection of nearly 200,000 books, taken from the library of the private torrent tracker Bibliotik.

However, recent deposition testimony from a former Meta researcher tells a different story, according to the rightsholders.

Books3 Torrenting Testimony

In a joint status report filed with Meta on Tuesday, the rightsholders say that Stephen Roller admitted during a deposition last week that he torrented Books3 and knowingly distributed it. Roller worked at Meta between 2017 and 2023, and the download took place during that period, they say.

Roller didn’t recall exactly when he acquired the dataset, the plaintiffs note. He did acknowledge that Books3 was created in 2020, and that he didn’t work for any other company while at Meta.

This is relevant, as the court ruled last year that training Llama on books was fair use, leaving Meta’s BitTorrent downloads as the main open issue in the authors’ case. Earlier this month, a judge ordered Meta to name the employees who approved torrenting from shadow libraries.

Meta has acknowledged using Books3 before. In early 2024, it admitted that it used portions of the dataset to train its Llama 1 and Llama 2 models. That admission didn’t say how Meta obtained the dataset.

Roller also testified that Meta had copies of Books3 by the time he left its AI research group FAIR, the plaintiffs write. He also named two research scientists who, they say, likely acquired their own copies.

Roller no longer has his own copy. According to the plaintiffs, he deleted it about a year ago, possibly after he was subpoenaed for the second time. He did so “[d]ue to all this litigation,” as “it seem[ed] contentious to have copies of The Pile [which includes Books3].”

Books3 testimony

The claim that Meta had multiple copies, at least one of them torrented, was news to the plaintiffs, they write. They plan to ask Meta how many copies of Books3 it acquired and how, and will ask the court to step in if that fails.

Meta: Could Have Been for Himself

Meta sees things differently. The company notes that the status report is the first time the rightsholders raised these concerns, and the tech giant argues that Roller’s deposition doesn’t support them.

“Mr. Roller testified that he did not know when he downloaded a copy of the ‘The Pile’ via torrent, and did not testify that his download of the ‘The Pile’ was for Meta or at Meta, noting it could have been for himself or for another employer,” Meta writes.

Meta’s response

According to Meta, Roller also said that he didn’t know whether more than one copy was downloaded, or whether the two researchers he mentioned acquired Books3. He left Meta in January 2023 and has since worked for three other companies working on AI.

The deleted copy was stored on Roller’s personal computer, Meta adds. He removed it more than two years after leaving the company because he “didn’t need it, so [he’d] rather not have it.”

A (Pirated) Book Club

Books3 is not the only pirated material that comes up in the status report. The plaintiffs also suggest that pirated books may have been used at Meta for things other than AI training.

They want Meta to produce the contents of an internal Google Drive folder titled “ML Books”. In addition, they want records of a Meta book club that may have used books from shadow libraries.

In one of the documents Meta produced, an employee shared a “pirated book” with a colleague. “i know for vellum sake this is prob very ironic,” the employee wrote. When asked whether the book was pirated, the employee replied with a link to the “ML Books” folder.

The recipient told another colleague, “bro she tryna get me fired.” He added that he “may need her to delete those messages.”

ML Books

The plaintiffs see this as relevant. If Meta employees used shadow library books for a book club, that would impact Meta’s fair use defense.

However, Meta argues that this request comes too late. The plaintiffs first asked for the linked files on October 9, which was more than a month after the discovery period had closed.

As for the folder itself, Meta says it is investigating and will discuss it with the plaintiffs when it knows more.

Missing Server Logs

Roller’s copy of Books3 is not the only material the plaintiffs say is missing. Meta still hasn’t handed over all command history files from its torrenting, they note, despite court orders to do so. According to the plaintiffs, these logs show how Meta configured its torrent software and which torrent files it targeted, and thus which works.

Specifically, Meta has yet to hand over command history files from any of the servers it used during its torrenting periods, the plaintiffs say. They now ask the court to order Meta to say whether any of these files were deleted, and when.

Meta, in turn, counters that it has produced substantial quantities of logs from those servers and is still searching backups, handing over new files on a rolling basis. According to Meta, there is no reason to believe any command history files were deleted.

Entrepreneur’s case is scheduled to go to trial in the spring of 2027, with the other publishers lined up behind it, should it settle before then. Meanwhile, the list of related cases keeps growing. This month, publishers including Elsevier, Hachette and Macmillan, as well as more authors, joined the queue.

—

A copy of the joint case management statement, filed at the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, is available here (pdf).

item.title: Dutch Court Orders ISP to Block Z-Library and OceanofPDF
item.description:
Home > Anti-Piracy > Site Blocking >

A Dutch court has ordered Internet provider KPN to block shadow libraries Z-Library and OceanofPDF. The dynamic blocking order, requested by anti-piracy group BREIN, also covers new domains, proxies, and mirrors. Back in 2024, BREIN already said that it planned to target Z-Library if the site stayed online, and it kept its word.

In March 2024, the Rotterdam court added Anna’s Archive and Library Genesis to the Dutch pirate site blocklist.

The order was a win for anti-piracy group BREIN, but one prominent shadow library was missing. Z-Library wasn’t covered, even though BREIN warned in 2022 that it could seek blocking measures if the site recovered from the U.S. crackdown.

When we asked about the omission, BREIN explained that it focused on Anna’s Archive and LibGen because these were seen as more popular. The anti-piracy group added that it planned to request a Z-Library blockade in the future, if the site stayed online. More than two years later, BREIN has kept its word.

KPN Must Block Z-Library and OceanofPDF

Last Friday, the Rotterdam court ruled in BREIN’s favor in its case against Internet provider KPN. The court ordered the ISP to block Z-Library and OceanofPDF, which BREIN describes as the two largest and most popular book piracy sites that weren’t blocked yet.

The order lists one domain for OceanofPDF, oceanofpdf.com, and five Z-Library domains: z-library.sk, z-library.la, 1lib.sk, z-lib.gd and articles.sk.

OceanofPDF

According to BREIN, the shadow library sites offer tens of thousands of titles from Dutch rightsholders. These include books, magazines, (academic) journals, sheet music and newspapers.

BREIN adds that, when it served the summons, OceanofPDF had more than 200,000 monthly visits from the Netherlands, while Z-Library had over 300,000 Dutch visits per month.

BREIN sued KPN under the terms of the site blocking covenant, which it signed with several Dutch Internet providers in October 2021. This agreement requires BREIN to sue the providers in alphabetical order, and this time it was KPN’s turn.

While KPN was the only targeted ISP, other major Dutch Internet providers have agreed to follow suit under the covenant. These blocking actions are meant to make the shadow libraries much harder to reach in the Netherlands, at least without workarounds.

The covenant also required BREIN to try to take the sites offline at the source, before going to court. In July, BREIN asked the site owners, registrars, registries and hosting providers to take action, without result. According to the court, BREIN couldn’t be expected to do more.

Dynamic Order Covers Future Mirrors

The order has a dynamic provision, which allows for blocking actions against future domains, subdomains, proxies and mirrors. This means that if Z-Library or OceanofPDF switch to new domains to evade the blocking measures, BREIN can add these domains without going back to court.

KPN previously pushed back against a dynamic order. In 2023, the provider argued that a similar order targeting Lookmovie and Flixtor was too broad, but the court disagreed. This time, KPN didn’t put up a defense and left the decision to the judge.

Interestingly, Z-Library itself encourages people to run mirrors. Since 2025, users can operate mirror sites on their own domains and, since June, these mirrors can carry custom branding and be password protected.

Z-Library’s mirror page

Password-protected mirrors without any Z-Library branding are not easily detected by rightsholders, which makes them harder to block, also dynamically.

BREIN Points to Libraries

BREIN stresses that readers do not need these shadow libraries as there are plenty of legal options to get books.

“There are fantastic legal, user-friendly apps on the market that let consumers read and listen to countless ebooks and audiobooks. You can also borrow ebooks and audiobooks through the library at little cost,” BREIN writes.

“So there’s no reason at all to get books from illegal sources. Illegal services put all the revenue in their own pockets. Nothing reaches the authors and publishers.”

Whether the dynamic order can keep up with Z-Library’s network of user-run mirrors has yet to be seen, but it should make the sites harder to reach for casual visitors.

—

TorrentFreak has seen a copy of the latest blocking ruling issued by the Rotterdam court, but it has not been published publicly yet. BREIN’s announcement can be found here.

item.title: Funimation Shutdown Fuels Push for DMCA Exemption to Legally Rip Anime Content
item.description:
Home > Law and Politics >

When Funimation shut down in 2024, buyers of DVDs and Blu-ray discs that came with a Funimation digital release lost access to those copies. A fresh petition to the U.S. Copyright Office cites this as a reason for a DMCA exemption that would allow disc owners to make replacement copies for personal use. Rightsholders and other opponents of the proposal have until February to file their objections.

In April 2024, anime streaming service Funimation shut down its app and website, as it became part of Crunchyroll.

The closure also cut off access to the Funimation digital copies that came with DVDs and Blu-ray discs. This wasn’t well received by anime fans.

Today, Crunchyroll’s help page still states that it does not currently support these copies. Instead, the page encourages affected users to explore the anime streaming library that Crunchyroll does offer.

Funimation digital copies

The movies and shows are still on the discs and in theory American buyers could make their own digital replacement copies. However, doing so would break the law as the DMCA’s anti-circumvention provision prohibits bypassing the encryption on DVDs and Blu-rays, unless an exemption applies.

Petitions Seek New Disc Ripping Exemption

The U.S. Copyright Office reviews these exemptions every three years, and last week it opened ten proposed classes for public comment. Two of the underlying petitions deal with works for which digital access was discontinued, and one specifically mentions the Funimation case.

One of these petitions comes from Jayden Milne. He asks the Office to allow owners of DVDs, Blu-ray and Ultra HD Blu-ray discs to make a single secured, local copy for personal use, when the digital copy promised on the packaging is no longer available.

That covers two situations. The first are people who redeemed a digital copy before the service behind it shut down, as happened with Funimation.

The second are buyers of new discs whose code had already expired. According to the petition, Warner Bros. states that its digital codes expire based on a title’s release date rather than the purchase date, and that expired codes are not replaced. This means that a disc bought years after its release may come with a code that no longer works.

Milne’s petition

Milne wants owners of these physical discs to be able to rip a replacement from them, under strict conditions.

The replacement can’t be better than what was promised. If the box offered an HD digital copy, for example, owners can’t rip the 4K version. Also, the copy is for personal use and it must be destroyed if the disc is sold, given away or lost.

Disappearing Anime Streams

A second and related petition, submitted by Zakaria Zerhouane, focuses on anime more broadly. It covers series and films that were removed from authorized U.S. streaming platforms after their licenses expired, as well as anime released on disc by U.S. distributors that no longer exist.

The petition does not mention Funimation but lists several distributors, including ADV Films, Bandai Entertainment, Central Park Media and Geneon.

In addition to bypassing encryption on discs, Zerhouane also wants to legally circumvent the DRM, geo-locking, and session-based access controls that streaming platforms use. This is needed, the petition argues, as the anime licensing market is unstable.

“Streaming platforms provide no advance removal notice, preventing users from finishing or preserving works before they disappear,” Zerhouane writes.

Zerhouane’s petition

He adds that the consolidation of the U.S. anime market under “a single dominant entity” has made catalogs more volatile. The petition doesn’t name the company, but the description appears to fit Sony-owned Crunchyroll.

Neither petition covers all video content. Zerhouane’s request is limited to anime, while Milne’s only covers discs that came with a digital copy. Both petitions are restricted to personal and noncommercial uses.

Rightsholders Respond in February

The Copyright Office grouped these requests with four other ‘replacement’ petitions. These ask for personal backups of discs, including before they deteriorate, and permission to format-shift discs as playback hardware disappears. These become more relevant every year, as old formats decay.

The Office notes that the Register of Copyrights has repeatedly declined to recommend such format-shifting exemptions in the past. This means that, while they are on the agenda, approval is uncertain.

Before making any decision, the Office wants more details from stakeholders. It asks which copy protections are involved, whether the titles can be watched legally some other way, and why making these copies wouldn’t infringe copyright. It also wants to know whether allowing this would hurt sales.

Supporters have until December 7 to send in their comments. Opponents can respond until February 22, and public hearings will follow in the spring.

item.title: Vietnam Jails Pirate Football Streamers for Up to a Year, Three Escape Prison
item.description:
Home > Piracy >

A Vietnamese court has sentenced 14 people who worked on the pirate football streaming site Bún Chả TV, handing out the first prison terms we've seen since the country's piracy crackdown began earlier this year. Eleven defendants received sentences ranging from eight to twelve months, while three commentators got suspended sentences. The alleged organizer of the group does not appear to be among those sentenced.

In May, the U.S. Trade Representative opened a Section 301 investigation into Vietnam, arguing that the country’s piracy prosecutions lacked a deterrent effect.

USTR pointed to recent cases in which defendants received suspended sentences and relatively low fines. A few weeks earlier, Vietnam’s Prime Minister had ordered a nationwide crackdown on copyright infringement. Several criminal cases have since moved forward, including those against the alleged operators of HiAnime and the Xoi Lac TV sports streaming network.

Another site in the crosshairs was Bún Chả TV, which offered Premier League and Champions League streams with Vietnamese commentary. According to police, the site drew hundreds of thousands of visits a day.

Investigators described the site as an underground company, with separate teams for programming, commentary, SEO and accounting. The main revenue came from ads and from redirecting viewers to illegal gambling sites.

On May 15, police from several provinces moved in. They summoned suspects, searched homes and workplaces, and seized 38 computers and 42 phones. Less than two weeks later, Vietnam’s Ministry of Public Security announced that Bac Ninh police had charged ten people.

Up to a Year in Prison

That case has now reached a verdict. In a first-instance ruling reported last week, a court in Bac Ninh convicted 14 defendants of infringing copyright and related rights under Article 225 of Vietnam’s Penal Code, VTC News reports.

Four defendants, including the heads of the content, programming and operations teams, were sentenced to 12 months in prison. Five others received ten months, and two were sentenced to eight months.

Notably, three of the site’s commentators were not sent to prison. Their ten-month sentences were suspended.

Sentences per defendant, according to the verdict reports

Defendant Role Sentence
Đặng Thế Anh Content lead 12 months
Nguyễn Thế Anh Programming lead 12 months
Bùi Tiến Dũng Operations lead 12 months
Đinh Thọ Bình Commentator 12 months
Nguyễn Anh Đoàn Operations 10 months
Mai Nguyễn Nhật Minh Operations 10 months
Trương Đình Lộc Operations 10 months
Lê Xuân Sơn Commentator 10 months
Vi Quang Thiện Commentator 10 months
Vũ Ngọc Phát Operations 8 months
Hoàng Thụy Thúy Hằng Operations 8 months
Nguyễn Hoàng Nam Commentator 10 months, suspended
Lê Văn Tuyên Commentator 10 months, suspended
Khiếu Hoàng Anh Commentator 10 months, suspended

All 14 defendants reportedly admitted the charges and cooperated with the authorities. According to investigators, Bún Chả TV streamed more than 150,000 sports matches and it allegedly made more than 20 billion dong, roughly $760,000, in illegal profits from betting and gambling ads.

The defendants in court (photo: Công an Bắc Ninh)

The verdict reports don’t mention a total. Instead, they list illegal gains per person or team. The leader of the content team allegedly gained more than 430 million dong, while commentators made from more than 31 million to more than 480 million dong each.

‘Strong’ Penalties

The verdict was picked up by Rouse, the law firm that represents the Motion Picture Association in Vietnam. In an article headlined “Strong Vietnam criminal penalties,” published on Lexology on November 3, the firm calls the ruling another victory for Vietnam’s IP landscape.

“The defendants were all sentenced to terms of 8-12 months in prison,” Rouse writes.

From Rouse’s article

While Rouse is correct on the length of the terms, it doesn’t mention that three of the sentences were suspended. Instead, Rouse stresses that the ruling is part of a tougher enforcement trend.

“This ruling reflects a shift in enforcement strategy by Vietnamese authorities, who are increasingly moving past preliminary domain blocking to deliver criminal convictions against the operators of commercial-scale piracy rings,” the firm notes.

“This perhaps reflects the strength of the national crackdown following the USTR pressure in May,” the firm adds.

Organizer Not on Trial?

The 14 defendants worked on the site, but according to the indictment reported by VTC News, the operation was directed by Bùi Bá Hiến, who manages and runs a company called S24. Hiến allegedly instructed employees and hired collaborators to build and run Bún Chả TV.

Hiến is not among the 14 defendants named in the reports, as far as we can see. The reports don’t name any of the impacted rightsholders either.

Interestingly, in September, Bac Ninh police issued a wanted notice for a man of the same name, Bùi Bá Hiến, CEO of esports company Box Vietnam. This person is also charged under the same copyright statute.

Police said this man fled on May 13, two days before the Bún Chả TV raids, but none of the reports we’ve seen confirm that this esports executive is the same person that’s named in the Bún Chả TV indictment.

The USTR has until November 29 to make its Section 301 determination, although it can extend the investigation by three months if needed. On paper, Vietnamese law allows for sentences up to three years for copyright infringement. Whether the 8-12 month sentences are what Washington had in mind when it called for more deterrent punishments has yet to be seen.

item.title: Meta Employees ‘Interacted’ With Pirated Copies of Adult Films, Filing Shows
item.description:
Home > AI >

A newly unredacted court filing shows that Meta’s internal investigation found several employees who appear to have interacted with Strike 3’s adult films. The adult content producers say these were torrented copies listed in their lawsuit, but Meta says there is no evidence of torrenting. The company also stresses that the activity it identified was unauthorized and unrelated to its AI training.

Last year, adult film producers Strike 3 Holdings and Counterlife Media sued Meta, accusing the tech giant of downloading thousands of their films via BitTorrent to train AI models.

Meta denies the allegations. Early on, the company already suggested that employees or visitors may have downloaded the videos for personal use.

That position is now being put to the test in discovery. A joint status report, filed by both parties, shows that Meta’s own search turned up employees who appear to have “interacted” with the producers’ videos.

Employees ‘Interacted’ With Strike 3 Films

The status report was originally filed on October 21 with large parts blacked out. A week later, Meta narrowed the redactions, refiling a version that clearly shows what was previously hidden.

Before and after

According to Strike 3, Meta first shared the names of five employees who “interacted” with torrented versions of its films back in July. Meta says that this was a draft, sent by mistake, and clawed it back.

Five employees

Meta later shared the names again, but only for Strike 3’s lawyers to see. Strike 3 is not happy with this restriction, and in the status report it writes that the “Attorney’s Eyes Only” label limits its ability to investigate these individuals.

There may be more, too. Meta has told Strike 3 about additional employees who ‘interacted’ with the films and related torrent files, but it hasn’t named them yet. Why they are not named is not mentioned.

Meta, meanwhile, stresses that it has no evidence that the videos were torrented by these individuals or anyone else. According to the company, they “appear to have interacted with (e.g., viewed or opened)” Strike 3’s videos.

“To date, Meta has not found any evidence supporting Plaintiffs’ claims that the alleged torrent downloads were performed with Meta’s knowledge and authorization or for its benefit,” the tech company writes, adding that none of the activity listed in its interrogatory response was authorized or related to its AI training.

Third-Party IP Addresses

Meta also has an explanation for the IP addresses Strike 3 flagged. Most of the alleged downloads came from third-party IP addresses it has no control over, the company argues.

Meta’s own corporate IP addresses, meanwhile, mostly belong to an internet service it acquired years ago. This unnamed service was offered to the public and phased out in 2019.

While not mentioned in the legal paperwork, the Onavo VPN would perfectly fit this picture. This controversial service was owned by Meta until it was shut down in early 2019.

Meta: Alleged Pirate Had Already Left

The filing also brings some news on a separate case. In late August, Strike 3 identified an anonymous AT&T subscriber as a Reality Labs executive and asked the court to relate his “John Doe” case to the Meta lawsuit. Judge Eumi K. Lee denied that request without prejudice, as Strike 3 first needed permission to disclose his identity.

On October 15, Magistrate Judge Virginia K. DeMarchi granted that permission. After learning the name, Meta then informed Strike 3 that it will oppose a renewed motion, as this person had already left Meta at the time of the alleged torrenting activity.

Already left

Strike 3 disagrees, stating that it has “traced” John Doe’s copyright infringement to several years before he left the company. The adult producer still wants to relate these cases, but as far as we can see, it has yet to file a new motion.

For now, the employees’ names remain under the “Attorney’s Eyes Only” designation and kept away from the public. Whether their activity was as unrelated to Meta’s work as the company says has yet to be seen.

—

A copy of the joint case management statement, with Meta’s narrowed redactions, is available here (pdf).

item.title: Mexico’s Senate Approves ISP Rules to Disconnect Persistent Online Pirates
item.description:
Home > Law and Politics >

Mexico's Senate has approved copyright amendments that require Internet providers to have a policy to cut off repeat infringers, or risk liability for their subscribers' piracy. The law doesn't explicitly say who counts as a repeat infringer. The changes follow calls from U.S. rightsholders, and come months after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that ISPs aren't liable simply for keeping pirating subscribers online.

For years, record labels sued U.S. Internet providers that kept serving subscribers who were repeatedly accused of piracy.

This strategy took a major hit in March, when the Supreme Court wiped out the $1 billion verdict against Cox.

According to the Court, knowing about piracy and failing to act on it is not enough to make an ISP liable for contributing to it. However, south of the border, lawmakers have now taken a different approach.

On Tuesday, Mexico’s Senate approved a reform of the Federal Copyright Law that ties ISP liability to having a policy to terminate repeat infringers.

Senate Backs ISP Liability Rules

The Senate approved the amendments with roughly two-thirds of the vote, as the opposition voted against.

The Chamber of Deputies already approved the same text in October, so the decree now goes to President Claudia Sheinbaum. Her government proposed the changes in May to bring the law in line with the USMCA trade agreement between Mexico, the United States and Canada.

U.S. rightsholders pushed Mexico for ISP liability rules as well. In January, copyright industry coalition IIPA complained that Mexico’s 2020 reform “did not provide a clear principle of secondary liability for those inducing or promoting copyright infringement.”

In April, the USTR moved Mexico to a lower tier of its piracy watch list, citing the draft amendments.

Disconnect Repeat Infringers

The trade agreement also prompted an earlier change in 2020, when Mexico added DMCA-style safe harbors to its copyright law. As a result, hosting platforms and search engines are only protected if they have a policy to terminate the accounts of repeat infringers, but this didn’t apply to regular consumer ISPs.

The new amendments change that, requiring Internet providers to have a policy for terminating the service of repeat infringers. This policy has to be published permanently on their website and in their terms of service, and it must include a basic way to notify users.

New condition for Internet providers

In other words, what can be terminated is the Internet connection itself, not just an account. According to Mexican business outlet EL CEO, this means that access providers such as Telmex and Izzi will need such a policy.

Providers that don’t comply risk facing liability.

Under the new rules, any ISP that fails to meet its safe harbor conditions becomes liable for its users’ infringements if it knowingly contributes to, induces, or causes the infringement.

The same goes for an ISP that can control the infringing user and profits directly from the infringement. In both cases, the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI) can fine the provider up to roughly 4.7 million pesos (~$250,000), depending on the infringement.

Who Is a Repeat Infringer?

The law doesn’t explicitly define the term repeat infringer, nor does it say how many piracy accusations it takes before a subscriber can be cut off.

According to Aurora López-Portillo, director of legal services at IP firm ClarkeModet, each provider has to decide its own threshold. She told EL CEO that ISPs should also check whether the accusations actually hold up, while giving users a chance to respond, even though the law doesn’t require that.

During Tuesday’s Senate debate, some lawmakers in the opposition raised similar concerns. Senator Gabriel Elizondo warned that families can share a single connection, so the pirating activities of one person could leave an entire household offline.

Previously, opposition lawmakers proposed requiring a court order before Internet service could be suspended, but that proposal was not adopted.

Not Like Cox

In the U.S., the DMCA has a similar requirement too. ISPs that want safe harbor protection must implement a policy to terminate repeat infringers in appropriate circumstances. However, as the Supreme Court pointed out in the Cox case earlier this year, failing to meet that requirement doesn’t count against an ISP that argues it didn’t infringe.

“Under our precedents, a company is not liable as a copyright infringer for merely providing a service to the general public with knowledge that it will be used by some to infringe copyrights,” Justice Thomas wrote in the Court’s opinion.

Not liable

Mexico’s law uses a different route.

There, failing to meet the safe harbor conditions, including the repeat infringer policy, is the first requirement for liability. If an ISP also contributes to infringement with knowledge of it, or can control the infringer and directly profits from it, it can be held responsible.

The new repeat infringer rules will take effect 180 days after their publication in Mexico’s official gazette, which hasn’t happened yet as far as we can see. How Mexican ISPs will define a repeat infringer, and how many accusations it takes, has yet to be seen.

—

A copy of the amendments approved by Mexico’s Congress is available here (pdf, Spanish). The U.S. Supreme Court’s opinion in Cox v. Sony can be found here (pdf).

The Senate approved the amendments with roughly two-thirds of the vote, as the opposition voted against.

The Chamber of Deputies already approved the same text in October, so the decree now goes to President Claudia Sheinbaum. Her government proposed the changes in May to bring the law in line with the USMCA trade agreement between Mexico, the United States and Canada.

U.S. rightsholders pushed Mexico for ISP liability rules as well. In January, copyright industry coalition IIPA complained that Mexico’s 2020 reform “did not provide a clear principle of secondary liability for those inducing or promoting copyright infringement.”

In April, the USTR moved Mexico to a lower tier of its piracy watch list, citing the draft amendments.

Disconnect Repeat Infringers

The trade agreement also prompted an earlier change in 2020, when Mexico added DMCA-style safe harbors to its copyright law. As a result, hosting platforms and search engines are only protected if they have a policy to terminate the accounts of repeat infringers, but this didn’t apply to regular consumer ISPs.

The new amendments change that, requiring Internet providers to have a policy for terminating the service of repeat infringers. This policy has to be published permanently on their website and in their terms of service, and it must include a basic way to notify users.

New condition for Internet providers

In other words, what can be terminated is the Internet connection itself, not just an account. According to Mexican business outlet EL CEO, this means that access providers such as Telmex and Izzi will need such a policy.

Providers that don’t comply risk facing liability.

Under the new rules, any ISP that fails to meet its safe harbor conditions becomes liable for its users’ infringements if it knowingly contributes to, induces, or causes the infringement.

The same goes for an ISP that can control the infringing user and profits directly from the infringement. In both cases, the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI) can fine the provider up to roughly 4.7 million pesos (~$250,000), depending on the infringement.

Who Is a Repeat Infringer?

The law doesn’t explicitly define the term repeat infringer, nor does it say how many piracy accusations it takes before a subscriber can be cut off.

According to Aurora López-Portillo, director of legal services at IP firm ClarkeModet, each provider has to decide its own threshold. She told EL CEO that ISPs should also check whether the accusations actually hold up, while giving users a chance to respond, even though the law doesn’t require that.

During Tuesday’s Senate debate, some lawmakers in the opposition raised similar concerns. Senator Gabriel Elizondo warned that families can share a single connection, so the pirating activities of one person could leave an entire household offline.

Previously, opposition lawmakers proposed requiring a court order before Internet service could be suspended, but that proposal was not adopted.

Not Like Cox

In the U.S., the DMCA has a similar requirement too. ISPs that want safe harbor protection must implement a policy to terminate repeat infringers in appropriate circumstances. However, as the Supreme Court pointed out in the Cox case earlier this year, failing to meet that requirement doesn’t count against an ISP that argues it didn’t infringe.

“Under our precedents, a company is not liable as a copyright infringer for merely providing a service to the general public with knowledge that it will be used by some to infringe copyrights,” Justice Thomas wrote in the Court’s opinion.

Not liable

Mexico’s law uses a different route.

There, failing to meet the safe harbor conditions, including the repeat infringer policy, is the first requirement for liability. If an ISP also contributes to infringement with knowledge of it, or can control the infringer and directly profits from it, it can be held responsible.

The new repeat infringer rules will take effect 180 days after their publication in Mexico’s official gazette, which hasn’t happened yet as far as we can see. How Mexican ISPs will define a repeat infringer, and how many accusations it takes, has yet to be seen.
