Home > Opinion Articles >

In May, a Paris court ordered DNS resolvers to block six domains that streamed pirated tennis matches. After a series of quiet, unannounced expansions, the list has since grown to 118. This includes two domain names that now belong to TorrentFreak. Notably, no domain names have been taken off the list, not even one that was seized by the U.S. Government months ago.

On October 22, DNS resolver Quad9 announced that it will stop serving users in France, after a Paris court ordered it to block pirate tennis streams or pay a daily penalty.

The underlying order, which beIN Sports obtained in May, initially listed six domains. That number has since grown considerably, with the latest additions coming in late October.

To take a closer look at the evolution of this blocklist, we compiled it from the notices that Google files with the Lumen database when it receives a blocking order. Today, 118 domains are listed under this order.

From 6 to 118 Domains

The pirate site blocklist, which is one of many in France, expanded in batches. The first update, reported by Google on June 15, added 22 domains. Three more updates followed on September 21, October 16 and October 26, each adding exactly 30.

The blocklist snapshot, batch by batch

Reported to Lumen Domains added Running total Blocked by Google DNS in France (Oct 28) Blocked by Cloudflare DNS in France (Oct 28)
May 13 (court order) 6 6 6 0
June 15 22 28 22 0
September 21 30 58 30 0
October 16 30 88 30 0
October 26 30 118 3 0

Nothing appears to have been taken off the list. The notices only add domains, and the ones that no longer work were still blocked when we checked. The blocking measures remain in effect until November 14, when the WTA tennis season ends.

Transparency is limited and it’s hard for the public to see what is blocked and on what grounds. Arcom doesn’t publish blocking updates. Google’s Lumen notices are the only public record we found, and they take some digging. The later notices don’t mention the case number, so a search for the order only turns up the first few, and the full domain lists are only shown to people who request access from Lumen.

This example shows the value of the Lumen Database when governments or courts don’t provide transparency.

Quad9 didn’t block any of the domains before the court ruled on the penalty on October 21, according to the ruling, which records the foundation’s statement to that effect and beIN’s objections to it.

Expired Domains, Seized Site

ISPs, online intermediaries, lawmakers and rightsholders all have different views on the effectiveness and proportionality of site blocking. However, logically speaking, all should agree that there is no need to block a domain that no longer links to anything infringing. That’s not necessarily what happens.

We checked all 118 domains on October 28, from the Netherlands and through a French server. Most still resolve to an IP address. However, the exceptions are more interesting.

Four domain names no longer resolve at all. Two of these, predb.click and line.golden-iptv.in, aren’t registered anymore; the latter was one of the six domains in the original court order. Meanwhile, 4kib.xyz has been suspended by its registrar, and fermin37.com stopped working after we first checked it on October 23.

Another domain, fr4.sportplus.live, now loads a page titled “THIS DOMAIN HAS BEEN SEIZED”. Its main domain was among the pirate sports domains that U.S. authorities seized in July.

Seized globally, blocked in France

The mgntv-nexon.xyz domain, meanwhile, points to an IP address that belongs to domain marketplace Sedo.

In France, none of this makes a difference. Google’s DNS resolver blocks 91 of the 118 domains and NordVPN’s DNS blocks 89, dead names and all. The domains that aren’t blocked yet mostly come from the latest batch; only three of those 30 were blocked on October 28, two days after Google reported them. The exception is Cloudflare, whose 1.1.1.1 resolver blocks nothing. Cloudflare applies French blocking orders through its CDN instead, which a Paris court accepted as a reasonable effort in September.

We know all this because we looked at the DNS responses directly. Users that try to access these sites through a browser have no idea what is going on. They simply see an error message noting that the site can’t be reached. That also applies to rktv.top, which TorrentFreak owns today.

Browser error

Under New Ownership

On October 23, two names on the list were free to register for anyone, as they had expired. These are rktv.top, which was added to the blocklist in June, and ap-live.top, one of the six domains in the court order itself.

We registered both domains and put up a short page on each, stating that TorrentFreak owns the domain for research and that it doesn’t offer, link to, or promote any streaming service. That’s all.

TorrentFreak’s Research domain

From the Netherlands, this page loads as expected. In France, however, Google refuses to resolve rktv.top. “The requested domain is subject to a judicial injunction or other governmental blocking order for FR,” its DNS response reads. The response carries extended error code 16, which the DNS standard labels “Censored”.

Blocked in France

Some French ISP resolvers go a step further and redirect the DNS response. When we queried rktv.top through Bouygues Telecom and Free, the answer wasn’t a refusal but a different IP address, 54.246.190.12, which serves offrelegalesports.fr, a page that links visitors to licensed sports broadcasts. Completel, a business provider that belongs to SFR, gave the same answer. Orange’s resolvers, meanwhile, answered with 127.0.0.1, the address of the user’s own computer, or reported that the domain doesn’t exist.

In other words, a visitor who types in a domain that TorrentFreak owns, and that hosts a plain research notice, lands on an anti-piracy page instead.

Offrelegalesports.fr

The two research domains have been in place for two weeks and it seems that nobody noticed. We are not aware of an official appeal process for domain owners, as there apparently is no direct route to complain.

A Hong Kong Server

Finally, it is worth pointing out that most of the domains on the list point to Hong Kong. Of the 118 entries, 74 resolve to two IP addresses in a single Hong Kong range, and all of these domains return an “unauthorized” error when we try to load them.

Another 19 domains point to a second Hong Kong IP range. These all show the same page, titled “Service Premium — Online.” Together, that’s 93 of the 118 entries.

IP range (Hong Kong) Addresses, anonymized (domains per address) Domains What loads
103.211.100.x A (13), B (61) 74 “unauthorized” error
103.175.129.x A (3), B (2), C (2), D (2), E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N 19 “Service Premium — Online”
All other addresses 19 addresses 21 varies

What is hosted on these servers is unknown, as we didn’t try to access them. However, they are likely linked to a pirate streaming service, given beIN’s complaint. If anything, it shows that this blocking effort largely targets one or two streaming operations.

Thus far, the blocking efforts haven’t stopped them, in part because the operators can easily register new domains, as if it were Groundhog Day.

Meanwhile, France is preparing to step up its blocking efforts. In July, the French Parliament adopted a law that allows new domains to be added automatically during live broadcasts, with Arcom reviewing them afterwards. As far as we know, that doesn’t come with a transparency layer.

The current blocking order expires on November 14. Whether the domains on the list, including our two research domains, will be unblocked after that has yet to be seen.

item.title: Movistar Blocks Its Own Support Forum Under LaLiga Anti-Piracy Order
item.description:
Home > Anti-Piracy > Site Blocking >

Spain's court-ordered piracy blocking regime blocked the official customer support forum of Internet provider Movistar on Saturday night. A blocking notice referenced a ruling that LaLiga obtained together with the company that runs the Movistar Plus+ streaming service. On Sunday, the forum moved from Cloudflare to Amazon CloudFront, without any word from Movistar on why.

Every LaLiga match weekend, Spanish Internet providers must block hundreds of IP addresses that are linked to pirate football streams.

These blocks are the result of a December 2024 court order, obtained by LaLiga and Telefónica Audiovisual Digital, which broadcasts these matches on Movistar Plus+. The order targets Spain’s largest ISPs, including Telefónica’s own.

LaLiga is pleased with the blocking measures and said that they work as intended. However, they are not without controversy, as IP address blocks previously hit broader infrastructure including shared Cloudflare servers. On Saturday, this collateral damage landed in Telefónica’s own backyard.

Movistar Blocks Movistar

On Saturday evening, Movistar’s official forum became unreachable through several Spanish ISPs.

This Comunidad Movistar forum is where the ISP’s customers go for help with their routers, Movistar Plus+ programming, or to report outages. Shortly after 22:00, this support community became unreachable.

According to RedesZone, X user Alvaro Canteiro was the first to notice. At 22:17, he posted that LaLiga appeared to have blocked Movistar’s official forum, presumably as a side effect of its anti-piracy blocking.

Those who tried to visit the forum through rival ISP DIGI saw a blocking notice. It explained that the IP address was blocked under the December 18, 2024 ruling of the Commercial Court No. 6 in Barcelona, requested by LaLiga and Telefónica Audiovisual Digital.

Blocked (via @zombietoads)

DIGI wasn’t alone. Bandaancha reports that Telefónica routed the forum’s IP address into a black hole, leaving visitors in the dark, without any response at all.

Based on data from blocking tracker HayAhoraFútbol, RedesZone reports that all operators blocked the two Cloudflare IP addresses the forum used at the time. That included Movistar, which effectively blocked access to its own community.

Blocked Cloudflare IP addresses are nothing new in Spain. LaLiga started targeting them in February 2025, and site owners have complained about collateral damage on match days ever since.

item.title: Pirate Library WeLib Hit With $19.5m Default Judgment and Domain Takedown Order
item.description:
Home > Lawsuits > Apps and Sites >

A New York federal judge has awarded thirteen major publishers $19.5 million in damages in their lawsuit against pirate library WeLib. The default judgment also orders registries, registrars and hosting providers, including Cloudflare and Njalla, to take the site's domains offline. Whether the publishers will ever see any money is doubtful, as WeLib's operators have yet to be identified.

In June, WeLib became the second shadow library to be sued by the same group of book companies, after Anna’s Archive.

According to the complaint, the relatively young site was built on code and books that it copied from Anna’s Archive.

WeLib’s anonymous operators didn’t respond to the lawsuit, which prompted the publishers to request a default judgment last month. Their brief borrowed heavily from one they had filed against Anna’s Archive earlier this year, including a claim about BitTorrent that didn’t appear to fit the WeLib case.

After reviewing the paperwork, U.S. District Judge Victor Marrero nonetheless granted the request in full. In an order issued yesterday, he gave the publishers everything they asked for.

Maximum Damages

The judgment awards each of the thirteen publishers, which include Penguin Random House, Elsevier and HarperCollins, $150,000 per book for ten of their works listed in the complaint. That is the maximum in statutory damages for willful infringement, adding up to $1.5 million per publisher.

$19.5 million

The total of $19.5 million matches what Judge Jed Rakoff awarded against Anna’s Archive in May. While that is a big win, collecting it is another matter, as WeLib’s operators have not been identified.

The judgment does order the WeLib operators to come forward. In addition to destroying all unauthorized copies of the publishers’ works, they must file a sworn report within ten business days after being served, including valid contact information for WeLib and “each of its managing agents.”

Domain Takedowns

The judgment also includes a permanent injunction that prevents WeLib from making the publishers’ works available anywhere in the world. At the same time, it targets the infrastructure that keeps the site online.

All domain name registries, registrars and hosting providers for the site are ordered to permanently disable welib.org, welib.st and welib-public.org. They also have to disable the site’s nameservers and stop hosting it, while preserving any evidence that could identify the operators.

Domains and intermediaries

The order names five past or present providers specifically: Public Interest Registry, Cloudflare, Tucows and two Njalla entities. That said, it also applies to all other registries, registrars and hosting providers for WeLib’s domains, now or in the future.

Signed Word for Word

The judgment is identical to the proposed order the publishers submitted in October and Judge Marrero signed it without changes. That includes the clause preventing WeLib from enabling users or third parties to make the works available, “including via BitTorrent.”

Including via BitTorrent

As far as we know, there is no evidence that WeLib uses BitTorrent. The WeLib complaint doesn’t mention it either. The same clause appears in the earlier default judgment against Anna’s Archive, where the complaint described the site’s dedicated “Torrents” page.

Still Online

With the injunction in hand, the publishers will likely ask intermediaries to take action. This includes the Public Interest Registry, which manages the .org domain and is based in the United States. Foreign intermediaries may not all comply with an American court order, however.

At the time of writing, welib.org and welib.st still load the familiar search page, advertising 43 million books and 98 million articles.

WeLib, still online

Anna’s Archive also lost several domains to an earlier injunction, obtained by music companies. However, it remains online through .gl, .pk and .gd domains, which are tied to registries and registrars outside the United States.

Whether WeLib plans to copy the moves of Anna’s Archive has yet to be seen, but given its history that would not be a surprise.

—

A copy of the default judgment, signed by Judge Victor Marrero on November 9, 2026, is available here (pdf). The publishers’ proposed order can be found here (pdf).

item.title: Nintendo Targets Picofly Switch Modchip Firmware in GitHub DMCA Takedown
item.description:
Home > Anti-Piracy > DMCA >

After taking down Switch emulators and hacking tools on GitHub for years, Nintendo is now going after modchip firmware. The gaming company sent a DMCA notice targeting firmware for modchips such as Picofly, SX Core and HWFLY, after which GitHub disabled 144 repositories. To back its claim, Nintendo cites the criminal case against alleged Team-Xecuter members, which led to a guilty plea from one of its three defendants.

In 2020, Nintendo went to court to stop the sale of SX Core and SX Lite, two Team-Xecuter modchips designed to work on all Switch consoles at the time.

These lawsuits were followed by a criminal prosecution in the United States, and Team-Xecuter’s operation effectively shut down. The chips lived on, however, and remained available through compatible alternatives such as HWFLY and Picofly.

Now, Nintendo is also going after the repositories that host the firmware for these modchips.

In a takedown notice dated November 6, which GitHub published on Tuesday, Nintendo of America targets Ansem-SoD/Picofly. According to its description, this repository offered information and firmware for a Switch modchip based on the RP2040-Zero board.

Picofly

The notice names only the parent repository, but its effect doesn’t stop there. Because the network was larger than a hundred repos and Nintendo said that all or most forks are infringing, GitHub disabled the entire network of 144 repositories.

From Emulators to Modchips

Nintendo’s earlier GitHub notices mostly went after emulators, key dumping tools and so-called sigpatches. This time, the gaming giant targets repositories offering firmware for SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly and HWFLY modchips.

According to Nintendo, the Switch’s technological protection measures (TPMs) include the console’s boot sequence and various cryptographic signatures. The company says the modchip firmware bypasses that boot sequence, violating the DMCA’s anti-circumvention provisions.

“The firmware allows Nintendo Switch modchips to illegally circumvent Nintendo’s TPMs in order to run illegal copies of Nintendo Switch games,” the notice reads.

From Nintendo’s notice

As far as we know, this is the first time Nintendo has targeted modchip firmware on GitHub. None of the 90 earlier Nintendo notices in GitHub’s public archive mention modchips. The closest are the 2023 and 2024 notices against key dumping tools such as Lockpick_RCM.

A Team-Xecuter Precedent

To support its circumvention claim, the notice points to the criminal case No. 2:20-cr-00127-RSL. That’s the case against the alleged members of Team-Xecuter.

The U.S. indicted three people in 2020. One of them, Gary Bowser, pleaded guilty to conspiring to circumvent technological measures and to traffic in circumvention devices. He was later sentenced to 40 months in prison.

The other two defendants, including alleged leader Max Louarn, have not appeared before the U.S. court as far as we know, and both remain at large.

It’s worth noting that Bowser’s guilty plea is not a court ruling on modchip firmware. However, at the takedown stage, Nintendo doesn’t need one, and GitHub appears to have processed the notice regardless.

Firmware Still Online

When we checked on Wednesday, the Picofly repository was replaced by GitHub’s standard takedown message, which also explains that the owner can file a counter notice.

Repository unavailable

However, not all modchip firmware is gone. Several other GitHub repositories with Picofly and HWFLY firmware were still online, including what a GBAtemp forum user describes as the original Picofly source. None of these are named in Nintendo’s notice.

Nintendo also sent three emulator notices on the same day. One targets the Citron Neo emulator, where GitHub disabled a network of 71 repositories, and two target single copies of yuzu.

Nintendo’s November 6 notices (published later)

Repository Project Repos Status
Ansem-SoD/Picofly Picofly firmware 144 Disabled
citron-neo/emulator Citron Neo 71 Forks disabled
IpwnedU/yuzu-mainline-master yuzu 1 Code removed
IpwnedU/yuzu-android-master yuzu 1 Code removed

These yuzu repositories are still on GitHub, but their owner has since removed the code and cleared the commit history. Both now only host a README which says that the source code can be found on the Internet Archive.

For now, the Picofly network remains offline. Its owner can still file a counter notice, but GitHub’s archive shows no sign of one yet.

—

Nintendo’s DMCA notice targeting the Picofly repository is available at GitHub here. The Citron Neo notice can be found here, and the two yuzu notices here and here.

item.title: Copyright-Strike-for-Hire: Lawsuit Targets Service Over Fake Meta Takedowns
item.description:
Home > Anti-Piracy > Takedowns and Seizures >

A rivalry between two Miami sellers of $120 dog breed photo books has been escalated to a Florida federal court. The lawsuit accuses a rival publisher of hiring an account-ban vendor, who allegedly weaponized Meta's copyright system by filing takedown notices in the target's own name. The takedown vendor later offered to withdraw the strikes and share his client’s details if the bookseller deactivated its pages for 30 hours, so he could get paid.

Earlier this year, we reported how scammers allegedly abused Meta’s Rights Manager to claim other creators’ videos and hit their accounts with copyright strikes.

Regular DMCA takedown notices can do similar damage. Meta’s takedown emails remind users that it terminates the accounts of repeat infringers “when appropriate,” which turns false notices into an effective weapon.

According to a lawsuit filed in Florida federal court last week, that weapon can be hired too. This lawsuit’s backstory involves two dog book publishers and a takedown contractor who tried to play both sides.

A Dog Eat Dog Playbook

The complaint was filed by The Everything Editions LLC, which sells photo books of various dog breeds for $120 each under the name The Dog Book.

Rival publisher Remus Collection is one of the defendants in this case. This company also sells dog breed books for $120, and in August it accused The Dog Book of infringing its copyrights. The Dog Book disputed this and, among other things, questioned whether Remus’s own website copy was written by a human or by an AI tool.

Interestingly, The Dog Book’s own Instagram features several posts of books and images that have an ‘AI content’ label, but that’s beside the point.

Remus (top) and The Dog Book (bottom)

Remus never answered those questions, according to the complaint. Instead, a Remus principal and others asked their Instagram followers to report The Dog Book “for scam/fraud.” This apparently worked, as Instagram suspended The Dog Book’s account on September 7, citing its account integrity standards.

After a cease and desist letter, Remus’s lawyer agreed in writing that Remus would stop calling The Dog Book a scam or fraud, the complaint notes. However, that didn’t end the matter, and the complaint alleges that the attack continued underground.

Monetized Copyright Strikes

The Dog Book opened new Instagram accounts, but these were reported and disabled too, the complaint says. The first replacement went down on September 9, a day after Remus’s lawyer agreed to stop.

In early October, Meta received six copyright notices targeting The Dog Book’s Instagram posts. These included photos and videos of Yorkshire Terriers, Dachshunds, a Cocker Spaniel and a Jack Russell.

Interestingly, these notices were filed in the name of The Dog Book itself. They all listed “The dog book” as rightsholder, while claiming to own the bookseller’s posts.

‘Rights Owner: the dog book’

Meta took action in response to these notices, adding to The Dog Book’s continued trouble. According to the complaint, the takedown actions were the work of a hired gun, who surprisingly tried to play both sides.

Takedown Vendor Plays Both Sides

In mid-October, a man using the name “Ashmit Ashmit” reached out to The Dog Book’s Facebook page, claiming responsibility for the copyright strikes on its accounts. He also came with a proposal.

“One guy need to ban your fb and ig both. He his paying me 1k doller. I also strike cpr on your accounts i will take all back and i have a good plan if you agree,” he wrote.

The conversation then moved to Telegram, where the contractor uses the handle “Fix My Brand.” His good plan required The Dog Book to take its own social media accounts offline.

The good plan

In other words, if The Dog Book went dark for 30 hours, the contractor could collect the money from his client and then withdraw the strikes.

Playing Along

According to its own messages, The Dog Book played along at least once and took its pages offline during a weekend. That didn’t go as planned, however, as the contractor complained that the pages came back too soon. As a result, he didn’t get paid by his client.

“You do 18 hour i dont get my payment. Okay if you are not in a mood boss no issue. I will take down your ig now when you get in your mood let me know after your ig burn,” he wrote.

The bookseller, meanwhile, wanted names of those who requested the takedowns. When it listed Remus and its principals, the contractor answered “Yes.” Later, he wrote that if his clients found out, “they will cancle all my deals.”

To back up his story, he forwarded messages from the person who, according to the complaint, was directing the takedown spree. One of these messages clearly states what the payment was for.

Forwarded messages

“THE PAYEMNT IS FOR DEFINTIVE BAN,” it reads.

Still in Business

According to the complaint, “Fix My Brand” is a commercial vendor selling account suspensions, who also runs the Telegram channel “FMB Vault.” This channel is still online at the time of writing, with 199 subscribers and a biography that now describes the operator as a “Specialist in Account Ban + Unban.”

FMB Vault’s Telegram

Meanwhile, The Dog Book says the campaign continues. According to the complaint, its Facebook accounts were reported more than four hundred times in recent weeks, with someone claiming that they showed sexually explicit content.

“Plaintiff’s accounts contain no sexually explicit content of any kind, and never have. Plaintiff’s accounts display photographs of dogs and of photographic books about dogs, together with product information and ordinary commercial marketing copy,” the complaint clarifies.

The Dog Book accuses the defendants of DMCA misrepresentation, false advertising and defamation, among other claims, and puts its losses at more than $600,000.

None of these allegations have been tested in court, and the defendants have yet to appear in the case.

False copyright claims and blackmail-esque schemes on social media are nothing new. However, as far as we know, this is the first U.S. lawsuit that targets a vendor who allegedly sells takedowns and suspensions as a service.

—

A copy of The Dog Book’s complaint is available here (pdf). The exhibits with the copyright notices, Telegram messages and Instagram stories can be found here (pdf).

To back up his story, he forwarded messages from the person who, according to the complaint, was directing the takedown spree. One of these messages clearly states what the payment was for.

Forwarded messages

“THE PAYEMNT IS FOR DEFINTIVE BAN,” it reads.

Still in Business

According to the complaint, “Fix My Brand” is a commercial vendor selling account suspensions, who also runs the Telegram channel “FMB Vault.” This channel is still online at the time of writing, with 199 subscribers and a biography that now describes the operator as a “Specialist in Account Ban + Unban.”

FMB Vault’s Telegram

Meanwhile, The Dog Book says the campaign continues. According to the complaint, its Facebook accounts were reported more than four hundred times in recent weeks, with someone claiming that they showed sexually explicit content.

“Plaintiff’s accounts contain no sexually explicit content of any kind, and never have. Plaintiff’s accounts display photographs of dogs and of photographic books about dogs, together with product information and ordinary commercial marketing copy,” the complaint clarifies.

The Dog Book accuses the defendants of DMCA misrepresentation, false advertising and defamation, among other claims, and puts its losses at more than $600,000.

None of these allegations have been tested in court, and the defendants have yet to appear in the case.

False copyright claims and blackmail-esque schemes on social media are nothing new. However, as far as we know, this is the first U.S. lawsuit that targets a vendor who allegedly sells takedowns and suspensions as a service.
